title: Developer Quickstart Phrases and Pricing Ladders
summary: Working draft of short, developer-facing quickstart copy plus suggested pricing ladder language and tactical rebuttals for sales/dev advocates. Focus: fast integration, predictable perf, and clear escalation paths for budget-conscious engineers.
background: We have many existing long-form assets about developer onboarding. This doc is intentionally concise — a set of single-sentence hooks and short pricing concession ladders that can be A/B tested in kickoff emails, docs hero banners, and in-app onboarding flows.
target_audience: Software engineers and ML engineers evaluating hosted inference for early-stage product features; usually building PoCs or first production rollouts with limited ops bandwidth.
key_value_props: Integrate in minutes with a single SDK and example app — shipping a call to generate text in <10 lines>, no infra required.
Predictable tail latency: perf profiles exposed per model so engineers can choose cost/latency tradeoffs with confidence.
Local dev parity: mock server + offline dev tooling so you can iterate without burning credits or waiting on cloud deployments.
Fail-safe routing: automatic fallback to cheaper/compatible model variant under capacity pressure, preserving availability.
Transparent economics: token-level cost breakdowns in the console and SDK hooks so you can instrument per-endpoint spend early.
quickstart_angles: 10-line integration: show the absolute minimum to make a request and display output in a dev console.
From idea to demo in 30 minutes: quick templates for chatbots, note summarizers, and search re-rankers with sample prompts.
Local-first dev: how to run a mock server + test harness so CI runs without calling the hosted endpoint.
Measure-first approach: ship with a cheap model variant + perf telemetry, then flip to a higher-quality model behind a feature flag.
Cost-safety built-in: example snippet showing request-level cost caps and graceful fallbacks to a cached answer.
example_quickstart_snippet:
Example minimal flow:
1) install: pip install redwood-client
2) set env REDWOOD_API_KEY
3) minimal call:
from redwood import Client
client = Client()
resp = client.generate(
  model="xlight-2.1",
  prompt="Summarize the following customer email:
---
I need a refund..."
)
print(resp.text)
pricing_language: Starter: Free tier with 100k tokens/month for experimentation — ideal for prototypes and demos.
Pay-as-you-go: flat per-token price with explicit per-request cost field returned in headers for immediate billing visibility.
Volume tiers: automatic discounts at 1M and 10M tokens/month; billed monthly, discounts apply retroactively for the billing period.
Committed capacity: reserved pools for steady throughput with lower unit prices and SLA credits for outages.
Burst protection: short bursts above reserved capacity routed to a best-effort pool rather than failing requests — configurable per account.
Concession ladder (for sales): trial credits -> 3 month pilot commitment (15% discount) -> 12 month committed (25% discount + onboarding credit).
objections_and_replies: Objection: 'Hosted APIs are expensive at scale' -> Reply: 'We show per-token unit economics and suggest a hybrid approach: start hosted + move predictable high-volume paths to Dedicated with identical API and tooling.'
Objection: 'Latency spikes worry me' -> Reply: 'We expose tail-latency SLIs per model and recommend early telemetry routes; can pin to dedicated capacity for strict SLOs.'
Objection: 'We need data control' -> Reply: 'Private deployments and VPC options available; same API shape so migration is straightforward.'
competitive_landscape_bullets: Large cloud providers: strong on infra and integration with existing cloud accounts but often slower to publish model perf profiles and lack single SDK experience across hosted vs private.
Closed-model APIs: may feel simple but opaque costs and flaky performance at scale — good positioning for us: transparent perf + model catalog comparisons.
Open-source runtimes/self-host: attractive on unit cost but requires ops/build time; pitch Redwood as 'go fast now, optimize later' with clear escape-hatch to private/de-dicated modes.
Inference specialists: good at raw throughput; our advantage is developer ergonomics (samples, quickstarts, local mocks) and productized cost controls.
rollout_recommendations: Test quick phrases in onboarding emails and docs banner A/B: 'Integrate in 10 lines' vs 'Ship a demo in 30 minutes'.
Surface per-request cost header in SDK logs by default during trial to educate teams about economics early.
Bundle a 30-day, low-friction pilot that auto-expands to PAYG unless the team opts into committed capacity (clear upsell path).
Equip sales with a one-page pilot checklist: success metrics, expected token volume, perf target, and fallback plan.
open_questions: What exact free-tier token count maximizes conversion without encouraging long-term freeloaders?
Do we pilot a mandatory perf telemetry snippet for all new keys to gather baseline tail-latency data?
Should burst protection be on by default for starters or opt-in per account?
